questions.question: What is a Helm chart?

options.text: A dashboard showing only CPU usage.
A package of templates and configuration used to define Kubernetes resources.
A replacement for container images.
A physical machine in a cluster.

questions.explanation: A Helm chart packages related Kubernetes resource templates, default values and metadata so an application can be installed and configured consistently.

questions.question: What is the purpose of values.yaml in a typical Helm chart?

options.text: To store every application's runtime logs.
To replace the Kubernetes API.
To build the application's container image.
To provide default configuration values used by the chart's templates.

questions.explanation: values.yaml supplies default template values, such as an image tag or replica count. These defaults can be overridden for a particular installation or upgrade.

questions.question: The same application needs different replica counts in development and production. Which approach supports reuse of one Helm chart?

options.text: Use separate environment values files that override the replica count.
Manually edit running Pods after every deployment.
Remove the replica count from all configuration.
Require development and production to use identical resources.

questions.explanation: Environment-specific values files allow the same chart templates to be reused with different settings, reducing duplication.

questions.question: Why inspect the Kubernetes manifests rendered from a Helm chart before deploying?

options.text: Rendering guarantees that the application has no bugs.
Rendering automatically tests every external dependency.
It helps verify that templates and values produce the intended resource configuration.
It removes the need for deployment permissions.

questions.explanation: Reviewing rendered manifests can reveal unexpected names, image references or configuration. Runtime behavior still needs separate validation.

questions.question: Which sequence is a reasonable application delivery pipeline?

options.text: Deploy to production, delete the source code, then run tests.
Run tests, build and publish a versioned image, deploy it, then verify application health.
Skip tests and manually modify every production container.
Publish credentials in the repository, then deploy.

questions.explanation: A delivery pipeline checks the code, creates a deployable artifact, deploys that artifact and verifies the resulting application.

questions.question: An image has passed staging tests. What best ensures production receives exactly the same image artifact?

options.text: Rebuild the image from whichever source code is newest.
Use any image carrying the latest tag.
Edit the image manually before deployment.
Deploy the tested image using its immutable digest.

questions.explanation: An image digest identifies specific image content. Promoting that digest avoids accidentally deploying a different build or a tag that has changed.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a readiness probe during application delivery?

options.text: To indicate whether a container is ready to receive application traffic.
To compile the application.
To replace all unit tests.
To guarantee that the application will remain healthy forever.

questions.explanation: Readiness helps Kubernetes determine whether a Pod should receive normal Service traffic. It is distinct from checking whether a container should be restarted.

questions.question: Why should a release rollback plan consider database changes?

options.text: Rolling back application code always restores every database automatically.
Database changes cannot affect older application versions.
An older application version may be incompatible with the changed schema or data.
A rollback always requires deleting the database.

questions.explanation: Rolling back application resources does not necessarily reverse database migrations. Compatibility and data recovery need to be considered in the release plan.
